title: Ang 1197: Sarang begins
hook: Guru Ram Das opens the midday raga
tomorrow: how does a hymn cool someone down in the middle of a fight?

segments.voice: Yesterday, colored at home: Ramanand set out with sandalwood and found God in his own mind. That closed Basant. Turn the page, and the sun is straight overhead.

Noon in a heat wave. The sidewalk shimmers. The car's steering wheel is too hot to hold. Your shadow has shrunk to a puddle under your feet, and the only thought in your head is water, cold, now. Thirst at midday doesn't negotiate. On ang 1197 a new raga begins, Sarang, the raga tradition sets for the middle of the day. So what does the Granth sing when the sun is highest?
screen: `NOON IN A HEAT WAVE.` → `YOUR SHADOW, A PUDDLE.` → `WATER. COLD. NOW.`

segments.voice: It sings about leaning. In the fourth Guru's Sarang hymns, under the heading Mahala 4, the mind is told to repeat the Name of the Lord of the world, and the hymn says, in paraphrase: the Lord is my support, all day and all night. At midday that word, support, lands differently. It's what you want when the heat is pressing down: a wall to lean on, shade, something cool in your hand. The Name, in the Granth's language, is amrit, nectar, the drink that doesn't run out. Here's something to tell a friend tonight, and it's a thing you can actually taste. In summer heat, Sikhs set up a chhabeel: a stand by the road serving cold sweetened water, or a milky drink, free, to anyone passing. Drivers pull over. Kids carry trays to car windows. Nobody asks who you are or what you believe before handing you a cup. It's the midday raga turned into something you can hold: a cool thing, given at the hottest hour, to whoever's thirsty. Midday is when shade matters most, and when the hymns say the Name does too.
screen: `SARANG, THE MIDDAY RAGA.` · `MAHALA 4: MY SUPPORT, DAY AND NIGHT.` · `THE NAME AS AMRIT.` · `A CHHABEEL: COLD WATER, FREE.` · then, large: `MIDDAY.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of cool water and take one slow sip. Hold it in your mouth for a moment before you swallow, and feel the cold travel down. Then sit with the glass in both hands and let the coolness be the whole practice. If you'd like, read ang 1197 before you begin.
Ang 1197. Where Sarang begins, the midday raga, and the hymns call the Lord a support all day and all night.
Midday: the hottest hour, when you need something to lean on, and a cold cup handed to anyone. See you tomorrow.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape senses (midday heat and a sip of cool water carry Sarang; the chhabeel is the thing to taste).

Who opens Sarang: the outline says Guru Ram Das; the writer's recollection is uncertain whether Guru Nanak's chaupadas (apune thaakur kee hau cheree) or Mahala 4 (jap man jagannaath jagdeesaro… mai har har har tek sabh dinas sabh raatee) come first at ang 1197. The script avoids saying who opens and only says the fourth Guru's Sarang hymns call the Lord a support all day and all night. Please confirm and adjust.
'The raga tradition sets for the middle of the day': the outline's 'midday raga', hedged as tradition.
The chhabeel is described as a summer custom without tying it to a date or event; some tellings link it to remembering Guru Arjan, left out here on purpose (gentle for children).
v3 storyline: heat wave in camp week two; the kids run a chhabeel by the road and a passerby asks if it's only for Sikhs (a small unity beat).
